name: Reporting Culture

quiz.text: A colleague tells you they clicked a phishing link but have already changed their password. What is the right move?

answers.text: Report it, because a password change does not end an existing session or remove anything configured in the account
Nothing - they handled it, and repeating it would undermine them
Ask them to forward you the email so you can decide whether it was real
Wait to see whether anything unusual happens, then report

quiz.text: What makes a security report actionable rather than just alarming?

answers.text: Times, named accounts and what was entered where, with a clear line between what you saw and what you are guessing
A confident conclusion about what the attacker was trying to do
Naming who was at fault so the right person can be spoken to
Keeping it brief so the team is not slowed down

quiz.text: Why does an attacker create a mail forwarding rule within minutes of getting into a mailbox?

answers.text: Because it keeps working after the session is revoked and the password is reset, unless someone opens the rules list
Because it is the fastest way to read old mail
Because it hides their sign-in from monitoring
Because forwarded mail cannot be traced

quiz.text: You report something that turns out to be completely harmless. What has it cost?

answers.text: A few minutes of triage, which is the price of keeping reporting fast enough to be useful when it is not harmless
Credibility, which makes the next report less likely to be believed
Nothing, but it should be avoided so the team is not flooded
The reporter is expected to investigate first to avoid false alarms

quiz.text: What does a healthy reporting culture require from the organisation, rather than from the reporter?

answers.text: That the person who made the mistake is visibly not punished, and that the team is told so
A detailed reporting form so triage has everything it needs
Anonymous reporting as the default channel
Annual training that explains what counts as a security concern

steps.name: Marcus Talks Himself Out of It

email.message:
Morning all,

If you got a signing request this morning that looks like it is from Brannock Fabrication, bin it. I opened mine before I looked at the sender properly and put my password in on the page it went to. It just 404'd afterwards so I think it is a dud that did not work.

I am changing my password as soon as I send this, so we should be fine. Not worth dragging security into it over a broken link.

Marcus
email.subject: Ignore the Brannock signing request

steps.description: A message lands on the operations list. It is not addressed to you, and the person who sent it has already decided it is nothing.
steps.instructions: Read the message from Marcus.

steps.name: Three Things Marcus Is Assuming

highlighterTexts: "It just 404'd so I think it is a dud." A 404 is what a working harvester shows you once it has what it came for. The page has no reason to keep talking to you.
"I am changing my password as soon as I send this." That closes the front door, once he does it. It does nothing to a session already open, or to anything already set up inside the mailbox.
"Not worth dragging security into it." This is the actual risk in the message. The technical mistake was ordinary; the decision not to raise it is what buys the attacker time.

steps.description: Every sentence in that message is a reason not to report. Look at what each one takes for granted.
steps.instructions: Step through what the message assumes, then click Next.

steps.name: Open the Reporting Portal
steps.description: It is not your incident, you have no proof anything happened, and Marcus has said he does not want it escalated. Report it anyway. Sign in to the portal.
steps.instructions: Open the reporting portal and sign in.

steps.name: File What You Actually Know

variables.name: description
variables.correctValue: At 11:41 Marcus Ilving emailed the operations list to say he had opened a signing request that appeared to come from Brannock Fabrication, entered his Sentinel password on the page it opened, and then saw a 404. He said he was changing his password and did not think it needed reporting. I have not spoken to him and I am not assuming the page was malicious. Reporting it so the session and mailbox can be checked.

steps.description: Write down what happened and nothing else. No theory about whether the page was real, no judgement of Marcus, no apology for possibly wasting anyone's time. Times and facts are what make a report actionable.
steps.instructions: Fill in the report and submit it.

steps.name: Why That Report Is Useful

highlighterTexts: A time, a named account and what was entered where. That is enough to pull session logs without waking anybody up to ask.
"I am not assuming the page was malicious." Saying what you do not know keeps the report credible, and it is what makes false alarms cheap enough to be worth filing.
The person named is not contacted before the check runs. Reporting a colleague is not the same as accusing one, and a culture where it is treated that way is a culture where nobody reports.

steps.description: The value is not that you raised an alarm. It is that a responder can act on this without calling anyone first.
steps.instructions: Review what you filed, then click Next.

steps.name: What the Password Change Fixed

answers.text: Only a future sign-in with the stolen password; it does not touch a session already open or anything configured inside the mailbox
answers.explanation: A password change invalidates the credential, not the session token issued before it, and it certainly does not undo a mail rule. This is why 'I changed my password' is a reason to report, not a reason not to.

answers.text: Everything, provided he changed it before the attacker signed in
answers.explanation: It would - but he has no way of knowing whether he was first, and the timing is exactly what a session check establishes. Assuming you won the race is the same as not checking.

answers.text: Nothing at all; password changes are security theatre after a phish
answers.explanation: Too far the other way. Changing it is correct and necessary. It is just not sufficient, and it is not a substitute for telling someone.

answers.text: It stops the attacker reading mail, but not sending it
answers.explanation: There is no such split. Whatever the session can do, it can do both.

data.question: Marcus changed his password within half an hour of his email. What does that actually stop?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: He Was Already In
steps.description: Bob collected the password at 11:40 and used it at 11:47, six minutes after Marcus's email to the list, while everyone treated the matter as handled. The password change at 12:10 logged nobody out.
steps.instructions: Sign in with the harvested credentials.

steps.name: What He Reads First
steps.description: He does not browse. He searches for money, and the top of the inbox is already holding some.
steps.instructions: Open the invoice thread.

steps.name: Eighty-Four Thousand, Pending

highlighterTexts: A live payment instruction he can edit from inside a trusted mailbox. He does not need to forge anything; he replies in Marcus's name and swaps the supplier's bank details for his own.
This is why mailbox access is not a small breach. The mailbox is where the company keeps its proof that something was agreed.

steps.description: A supplier has just changed their bank details by email, and the payment has not gone out yet.
steps.instructions: Look at what the thread contains, then click Next.

steps.name: Persistence Costs Him Nothing
steps.description: Access can be taken away. A rule he leaves behind cannot, unless somebody goes looking for it.
steps.instructions: Create the forwarding rule.

steps.name: The Thing That Outlives the Password

highlighterTexts: Every message, forwarded out, then marked read and archived. Marcus sees a tidy mailbox and never notices the copy leaving.
The destination reads as a backup address for his own name. A rule that looks like housekeeping is the one nobody deletes.
A password change does not remove this. Nor does revoking the session. Somebody has to open the rules list and look.

steps.description: Sixty seconds of work, and it keeps paying after he is locked out.
steps.instructions: Review the rule he left, then click Next.

steps.name: The Window

answers.text: It sets how long the attacker keeps working, because containment cannot start before somebody says something
answers.explanation: Detection tooling may or may not catch this. The reliable clock starts when a human reports, which is why the speed of reporting is a control in its own right.

answers.text: It makes no difference; monitoring would have caught the sign-in anyway
answers.explanation: A sign-in with a valid password from a plausible location is close to invisible. Monitoring is a second line, not a substitute for the person who already knows what happened.

answers.text: It only matters if the attacker steals data; a mail rule is a minor issue
answers.explanation: The rule is the part that survives everything else. It is the difference between an incident that ends today and one that runs for weeks.

answers.text: It protects Marcus from disciplinary action
answers.explanation: It does the opposite. An incident traced back to an unreported click is far worse for the person than the click ever was, and a reporting culture exists precisely to make that trade obvious.

data.question: Marcus decided not to report. What is the practical effect of that decision?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: What Your Report Started

email.message:
Alice,

Thank you for filing this. Marcus had not raised it and we would not have looked.

There was a live session on his mailbox opened at 11:47 from a network we have never seen. It has been revoked and the account is locked pending a reset. Your report reached us at 14:12; the session was killed at 14:19.

One thing survives all of that. A forwarding rule was created on the mailbox at 11:52, and revoking a session does not remove it. It is still running. As service desk you have mailbox administration, so please delete it now.

Open mailbox rules

Security Operations, Sentinel
email.subject: SEN-4471 - session revoked, one thing left for you

highlighterTexts: Your report is the only reason anyone looked. The attacker's session is now revoked and the account locked, seven minutes after you filed.
The catch: a forwarding rule the attacker created survives a password change and a revoked session. It keeps copying mail out until someone deletes it.
The link goes to mailbox administration on the company's own mail domain, the place where the forwarding rule can actually be removed.

steps.description: The service desk queue moves on your ticket. Read what it bought, and what it did not.
steps.instructions: Read the response from the security team.

steps.name: Open Mailbox Administration
steps.description: The rule lives on Marcus's mailbox, not yours. Service desk holds mailbox administration, so sign in with your own admin account - the one action here that has to be attributable to you.
steps.instructions: Open mailbox rules and sign in.

steps.name: Delete the Rule
steps.description: The session is dead and the password is being reset. Neither of those touches this.
steps.instructions: Delete the forwarding rule.

steps.name: What the Rule Outlived

highlighterTexts: Two hours and thirty-nine minutes, and the last twelve came after the session was killed. Revoking the session did not stop the rule; only opening this page did.
Containment is not one action. Killing the session was the fast part; finding what it left behind is the part that only happens if somebody is looking.

steps.description: Read the line the page prints once the rule is gone.
steps.instructions: Review the confirmation, then click Next.

steps.name: He Comes Back

highlighterTexts: Signed out, password changed, rule gone. Everything he built this morning is worth nothing, and the invoice was paid to the right account.
None of that happened because he was detected. It happened because somebody who was not involved decided it was worth mentioning.

steps.description: He had the password, and until this afternoon he had the mailbox.
steps.instructions: Watch him return to the mailbox, look the page over and click Next, then step through the highlight and click Next.

steps.name: Seven Minutes Against Eleven Days

email.message:
Alice,

Closed. The Brannock payment went out to the real account yesterday afternoon.

For the record, the timeline:
  • 11:40 - credentials entered on the harvesting page
  • 11:47 - attacker signs in
  • 11:52 - forwarding rule created
  • 12:10 - Marcus changes his password, which changes nothing
  • 14:12 - you report it
  • 14:19 - session revoked
  • 14:31 - rule removed

He had two hours and thirty-nine minutes. Across the cases we see where nobody reports, we find out on day eleven, usually from the supplier asking where their money is.

Marcus is not in trouble. We have told him so, and we have told the team, because the next person needs to believe it.

Security Operations, Sentinel
email.subject: SEN-4471 closed

highlighterTexts: The timeline shows Marcus's password change at 12:10 changed nothing. What stopped the attacker was the report at 14:12, then the revoked session and the removed rule.
The attacker had about two and a half hours. Without a report, cases like this surface on day eleven, after the money is gone.
Marcus is not in trouble, and the team was told so. That message is what makes the next person willing to speak up.

steps.description: The service desk closes the ticket with the number that matters.
steps.instructions: Read the closing note.

steps.name: What Reporting Actually Buys
steps.description:
Reporting is not a courtesy to the security team. It is the control that sets how long an attacker gets to work.

The clock starts when somebody speaks, not when something happens. A valid password used from a plausible place is close to invisible. The reliable signal is a person saying what they did.

Changing your password is necessary and not sufficient. It does not end an open session and it does not remove what was configured inside the account.

Report what you saw, not what you concluded. Times, accounts, and what was entered where. Saying plainly what you do not know is what keeps a false alarm cheap.

A bystander report is not an accusation. Marcus was not disciplined, and the team was told so - because the next person to click something has to believe that before they will say anything.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

description: An incident nobody reports keeps running, however good the detection tools are. Learn why to report a colleague's slip even when they say it is handled, write a report that sticks to what you know, and see why a password change alone does not end an attacker's session.

actorDescriptions.bob: A threat actor who runs credential-harvesting pages dressed as signing requests, and who counts on the victim being too embarrassed to say anything.
actorDescriptions.alice: You are Alice, an analyst on the IT service desk at Sentinel Security Solutions. You are not the person who made the mistake today, which is exactly why what you do next matters.

name: General Incident Reporting

answers.text: Only events involving hackers actively stealing data
Any event that could compromise data, allow unauthorized access, or violate security policies
Only events that have already caused financial damage
Only events detected by automated security systems

quiz.text: When should you report a potential security incident?

answers.text: Wait a few days to see if it happens again before reporting
Only report if you're 100% certain it's a real attack
Report immediately - time is critical and false alarms are acceptable
Try to investigate and fix the issue yourself first

quiz.text: Which of the following are security incidents that should be reported? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Receiving a login alert from an unfamiliar location
Finding your laptop missing from your desk
A colleague asking for your password to 'help with a project'
Receiving a routine newsletter from your company
Noticing unfamiliar software installed on your computer

quiz.text: What information should be included in an incident report? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: What happened (factual description of the event)
When it occurred (date and time)
Your speculation about who is responsible
What systems or data might be affected
Any evidence or screenshots you have

quiz.text: Why is it important to use official reporting channels instead of just telling a colleague?

answers.text: Official channels create proper documentation and ensure the right people are notified immediately
It's not important - telling anyone is equally effective
Official channels are only required for major incidents
You should only use official channels if your manager is unavailable

quiz.text: After reporting a suspected credential compromise, what immediate action should you take?

answers.text: Wait for IT to tell you what to do
Change your password immediately using a strong, unique password
Continue working normally since you've already reported it
Delete all your emails to prevent further access

steps.name: An Unusual Alert

email.message:
Dear Alice,

We detected a login to your ClearView account from a new location:

Location: Jakarta, Indonesia
Time: 3:47 AM (your local time)
Device: Windows PC - Chrome Browser
IP Address: 103.147.xx.xx

If this was you, you can ignore this message. If you did not log in from this location, please report this immediately using our Incident Reporting Portal.

Best regards,
ClearView Security Team
email.subject: Login Alert: New Location Detected

steps.description: A Thursday morning like any other. Among the overnight mail is an automated security alert from ClearView's systems, reporting a sign-in to your account from somewhere you have never been.
steps.instructions: Open your email inbox and read the new security alert.

steps.name: Analyzing the Alert

highlighterTexts: The login occurred from Jakarta, Indonesia - a location Alice has never visited and has no connection to.
The time was 3:47 AM local time - Alice was asleep and could not have initiated this login.
The email warns: If you did not log in from this location, please report this immediately - this is exactly what Alice should do.
Was it a glitch? Should you wait and see? Or report it now? Waiting is the only option that costs anything: the account is either compromised or it is not, and the difference is measured in minutes.

steps.description: Alice examines the security alert carefully. Several details stand out as concerning.
steps.instructions: Review the highlighted email to understand the warning signs, then click Next.

steps.name: Deciding to Report
steps.description:
Alice recalls her security training. A security incident is any event that could compromise confidential data, allow unauthorized access, disrupt operations, or violate security policies.

The suspicious login clearly fits this definition. She decides to report it immediately using the link provided in the security alert.
steps.instructions: Click the Incident Reporting Portal link in the email to access the reporting system.

steps.name: Accessing the Incident Portal
steps.description: Alice opens the company's internal incident reporting portal. She uses her password manager to log in securely - a good habit that ensures she's using strong, unique credentials.
steps.instructions: Click the email field, then select your saved credentials from the autofill popup to log in.

steps.name: Selecting the Incident Type
steps.description: The incident reporting form displays several categories. Since Alice experienced an unauthorized login from a foreign location, she needs to select the appropriate incident type. The suspicious login from Jakarta is clearly an Unauthorized Access attempt.
steps.instructions: Select 'Unauthorized Access' as the incident type.

steps.name: Completing the Incident Report

variables.name: description
variables.correctValue:
I received an automated security alert at 8:15 AM today reporting a login to my account from Jakarta, Indonesia at 3:47 AM local time. I did not authorize this login and was asleep at that time.

The alert indicated a Windows PC using Chrome browser. I have not shared my credentials with anyone and have not traveled recently. This appears to be unauthorized access to my account.

steps.description: With the incident type selected, Alice provides a clear, factual account of what happened, including the time, location data from the alert, and the fact that she did not authorize this login.
steps.instructions: Fill out the incident description with details about the suspicious login and submit the report.

steps.name: Immediate Response Actions
steps.description:
After submitting her report, Alice receives confirmation that the security team has been notified. The system recommends immediate steps: change your password and review recent account activity.

Alice knows that quick action can limit damage from a potential breach.
steps.instructions: Open your account settings on the portal and change your password.

steps.name: Changing Credentials
steps.description:
Alice uses the company's password manager to generate a strong, unique password. She knows that if her old password was compromised, changing it immediately is critical to preventing further unauthorized access.

The form requires her current password to verify her identity before allowing the change.
steps.instructions: Enter your current password, use the Password Generator to create a new secure password, and update your credentials. Then, click Next to continue.

steps.name: IT Team Response

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Thank you for reporting this quickly. We've reviewed the login attempt and confirmed it was not authorized by you. Here's what we've done:

- Blocked the IP address (103.147.xx.xx) from our systems
- Terminated all active sessions on your account
- Flagged the incident for further investigation

Early findings: your password shows up in an infostealer log, the output of malware that copies passwords as they are typed or saved on an infected computer. We are checking which device it came from.

Your quick reporting helped us respond before any data was accessed. Please continue using your new password and let us know if you notice anything else unusual.

We'll update you once our investigation is complete.

Best regards,
Marcus Chen
IT Security Team
email.subject: RE: Security Incident Report #2024-1847

steps.description: Within minutes, Alice receives a response from the IT security team. They've already begun investigating the suspicious login and have temporarily locked the foreign IP address from accessing company systems.
steps.instructions: Read the email from the IT Security team.

steps.name: Understanding the Response

highlighterTexts: The security team blocked the suspicious IP address immediately, preventing further access attempts from that location.
All active sessions were terminated as a precaution - this ensures that if the attacker was still connected, they are now logged out.
The password was copied by infostealer malware, not guessed. A strong, unique password does not help once malware has read it.
Nothing was hacked at ClearView: the attacker simply signed in. Reporting is what turned a valid sign-in into an incident somebody acted on.

steps.description: The IT Security team's response demonstrates how quickly the company can act when incidents are reported promptly.
steps.instructions: Review the highlighted email explaining the security team's actions, then click Next.

steps.name: What Reporting Bought
steps.description:
The sign-in was valid. The password was correct. Nothing at ClearView was broken into - which is exactly why no system was going to raise it with the security team, and why you had to.

Report before you are sure. Waiting to see whether it happens again is a decision to give an attacker the intervening hours.

Use the official channel. A portal entry is timestamped and routed; a message to a colleague is not.

Say what, when, and on which system. Specifics are what let a responder act without calling you first.

Then protect the account yourself. Changing the password is your half of the response, not a substitute for reporting it.

The same reasoning covers unusual system behaviour, unexpected installs, a lost device, a request for credentials, or mail from an account that is behaving oddly.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

description: A security event is worth reporting long before anyone is certain it is an incident. Learn to read an alert critically, choose the right incident category, write a factual report a security team can triage quickly, and take the first containment step alongside it.
